Rod Laver. An Australian tennis legend who remains the only player to win the calendar-year Grand Slam twice: in 1962 as an amateur and in 1969 as a professional. His extraordinary dominance in the 1960s redefined excellence in men's tennis and bridged the amateur-professional divide of the era. He won all four Grand Slam tournaments in a single calendar year in 1962, becoming the first player ever to accomplish this historic feat. He then accomplished the same thing again in 1969, making him the only player to achieve this remarkable double. A left-handed player known for exceptional speed, court coverage, and a powerful forehand, he won eleven Grand Slam singles titles overall during his career. In 1962 he turned professional, but then spent seven years banned from Grand Slam competition due to the strict amateur-professional divide that existed at that time. He was reinstated to compete in 1968, marking a turning point in tennis. He dominated the Australian Open, winning it six times across his competitive years, and was competitive at Wimbledon, the US Open, and the French Open. His competitive era roughly spanned from 1960 to 1974, overlapping with and ultimately overshadowing other notable players like Ken Rosewall and other contemporaries. The Australian Open's main stadium, Rod Laver Arena, is named in his honor.
